blocks.text: Cursor is built on VS Code, so everything in the VS Code tab works here: the same layout, extensions, `launch.json` and debug keys. What Cursor adds is three AI surfaces: Tab completion as you type, the Agent pane that edits many files, and inline edit on a selection. You have version 3.29 installed.

blocks.text: **One difference from VS Code.** Cursor uses `⌘` `K` for AI, so VS Code chords that start with `⌘` `K` start with `⌘` `R` in Cursor. Zen mode is `⌘` `R`then`Z`. Cursor changes quickly between versions; when a key here does not match, trust the shortcut list above.
Working with the agent like a pro

items: **Say where, what, and how you will check.** "In `@cart.ts`, the discount is applied as a multiplier instead of a percentage. Fix it and run the cart tests." beats "fix the bug".
**Plan first for anything over one file.** Read the plan, correct it, then let it edit.
**Read every diff.** Keep or undo block by block. An agent edit is a pull request from a fast junior, not a finished change.
**Rules save repeating yourself.** Project rules live in `.cursor/rules`; your global ones are in Cursor Settings → Rules → User Rules. Yours already tell Cursor to read `~/ai-handoff` first.
**Use checkpoints.** Each agent message has a restore point, so you can go back to the state before a bad turn.
**Paste the error, not a description of it.** Stack trace and failing command go in as text.
**Debugging with it.** Ask the agent where to put a breakpoint and what to look at, then run the debugger yourself. It reasons about the code; only the debugger knows the real values.

VS Code needs to be told how to start or join your program. That lives in `.vscode/launch.json`. **launch** starts the program under the debugger; **attach** joins one that is already running.

items: **Call stack (Frames):** the top line is where you are; each line below is who called it. Click a lower frame to see that caller's variables at the moment it made the call.
**Variables:** everything in scope. Values that just changed are highlighted.
**Watch:** expressions you pin so they stay visible as you step, such as `items.length`.
**Evaluate / console:** run any expression against the paused program. You can call functions and change values to test a fix before writing it.
**Threads:** mobile apps have many. UI work must be on the main thread; the stack tells you which one you are on.

blocks.text: **When a breakpoint is ignored.** Check, in order: you pressed Debug and not Run; breakpoints are not muted; the build is Debug, not Release; the running app was built from the code you are looking at; the debugger is attached to the right process (for BB Flutter that means Flutter Attach was waiting before the app started).

blocks.text: Drills

questions.q: Walk me through how you debug a problem you have never seen before.
questions.a: Reproduce it reliably first. Then state one guess about the cause and what value would prove it. Put a breakpoint or logpoint where that value is visible, compare what I see with what I expected, and narrow the area by halves. Fix the cause, not the symptom, then re-run the original steps and one nearby case to confirm nothing else broke.

questions.q: When do you use a debugger and when do you use logs?
questions.a: A debugger when I can reproduce the problem locally and need to explore values I did not think to print. Logs when pausing changes the behaviour (timing, animations, races), when the problem only happens on a user's device or in production, or when I need a history across many events.

questions.q: What is the difference between step over, step into and step out?
questions.a: Step over runs the current line, including any function it calls, and stops on the next line. Step into enters the function being called. Step out finishes the current function and stops in the caller. I step over code I trust and step into code I suspect.

questions.q: What is a call stack and how do you read it?
questions.a: The chain of function calls that led to the current line. The top frame is where execution is now; each frame below is its caller. I read downwards until I reach the first frame of my own code, and I click frames to see the variables each caller had.

questions.q: A bug disappears when you attach the debugger. What does that tell you?
questions.a: It depends on timing. Pausing or slowing one thread hides a race condition, or a debug build initialises memory differently from release. I switch to logpoints or plain logs with timestamps and thread names, and run a thread sanitizer if the platform has one.

questions.q: How do you find a bug that appeared sometime in the last 200 commits?
questions.a: git bisect. Mark a known good commit and a known bad one; Git checks out the middle, I test, and mark it good or bad. About eight rounds find the exact commit.

questions.q: Why would a breakpoint not be hit?
questions.a: The app was started with Run instead of Debug, breakpoints are muted, the build is release with optimisation, the running binary was built from older code, the debugger is attached to a different process, or the line genuinely never executes.

questions.q: What is the difference between launch and attach?
questions.a: Launch starts the program under the debugger. Attach connects the debugger to a process that is already running, which is needed when something else starts it: a native app hosting Flutter, a server in Docker, or a browser.

questions.q: What is a conditional breakpoint and when is it worth using?
questions.a: A breakpoint that pauses only when an expression is true, for example item.id == 4021. It is worth it when the line runs many times and only one pass is wrong. The condition is evaluated on every pass, so in a very hot loop it slows the program.

questions.q: What is a logpoint?
questions.a: A breakpoint that prints a message and continues without pausing. It gives me print debugging with no code change, nothing to remove afterwards and no rebuild. Xcode calls it a Log Message action with auto-continue; IntelliJ calls it a non-suspending breakpoint with Evaluate and log.

questions.q: What is an exception breakpoint?
questions.a: It pauses at the line that throws, before the stack unwinds, so I see the state that caused the error instead of the crash report afterwards. I keep one on for uncaught errors all the time and enable caught ones when an error is being swallowed.

questions.q: What is a watchpoint or data breakpoint?
questions.a: It pauses when a variable's value changes, whichever code changes it. I use it for the question 'who is modifying this?'. It is implemented with hardware support, so only a few can be active at once.

questions.q: What is a symbolic breakpoint?
questions.a: A breakpoint on a function name instead of a file and line. It works for code I have no source for, such as UIViewController viewDidAppear, and tells me whether and from where a framework method is called.

questions.q: A breakpoint in a server pauses and every other request hangs. Why?
questions.a: The breakpoint suspended all threads. Setting it to suspend only the current thread lets the rest of the server keep handling requests.

questions.q: What is the difference between po, p and v in LLDB?
questions.a: v reads the variable straight from memory without running code, so it is fastest and safest. p compiles and evaluates an expression and prints it with its type. po does the same and then calls the object's debug description, which is the most readable but runs the most code.

questions.q: How do you find a retain cycle?
questions.a: Reproduce the screen, dismiss it, then open the Memory Graph debugger. Objects that should be gone are still listed, and the graph shows the strong references keeping them alive. The fix is usually a weak or unowned capture in a closure or a weak delegate. Instruments Leaks confirms it over time.

questions.q: A view is not visible on screen. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Debug View Hierarchy. It shows every view in 3D with its frame, so I can see whether the view exists, has zero size, is off screen, is hidden or transparent, or is covered by another view. Then I check constraints in the size inspector.

questions.q: How do you change behaviour while paused without rebuilding?
questions.a: In the LLDB console, expr sets a variable or calls a method, for example expr view.backgroundColor = .red or expr isPremium = true, then continue. A breakpoint action can do the same automatically on every hit.

questions.q: What do the sanitizers do?
questions.a: Address Sanitizer catches memory errors such as use after free and buffer overflow. Thread Sanitizer catches data races. Main Thread Checker flags UI work done off the main thread. They are switched on in the scheme's Diagnostics tab and slow the app, so they are for debug runs.

questions.q: What is a dSYM and why does it matter?
questions.a: The file that maps addresses in a release binary back to function names and line numbers. Without the matching dSYM a crash report is only hexadecimal addresses; with it the report is symbolicated into a readable stack.

questions.q: How do you debug an app that is already running?
questions.a: Run → Attach Debugger to Android Process and choose the process. No rebuild or reinstall is needed, and it works at any point, which helps for bugs that take a long setup to reach.

questions.q: What is Logcat and how do you filter it?
questions.a: The device's combined log stream. I filter by package:mine to see only my app, by level:error for severity, and by tag: for a class. Crashes appear as a FATAL EXCEPTION block with the stack.

questions.q: What is an ANR and how do you investigate one?
questions.a: Application Not Responding: the main thread was blocked for about five seconds. I look at the main thread's stack in the ANR trace or pause the debugger and read the main thread's frames. The usual cause is disk, network or a lock on the main thread.

questions.q: Gradle sync fails. What do you check?
questions.a: The exact error in the Build window, then the Gradle version against the Android Gradle Plugin version, the JDK that Gradle is using, and whether a dependency could not be downloaded. Invalidating caches is the last step, not the first.

questions.q: What does the Layout Inspector show?
questions.a: The live view or Compose tree of the running screen with each node's properties and bounds, and for Compose how many times each composable recomposed. I use it for wrong sizes, overlaps and unnecessary recomposition.

questions.q: What is the difference between hot reload and hot restart?
questions.a: Hot reload injects changed code into the running Dart VM and rebuilds widgets while keeping state. Hot restart reloads the code and starts the app again from main, losing state. Changes to initState, global variables or enum definitions need a restart.

questions.q: How do you debug Dart code inside a native iOS or Android app?
questions.a: Attach rather than run. I start flutter attach so it waits, launch the native app in debug from Xcode or Android Studio, and the attach session connects to the Dart VM. Dart breakpoints then stop in the Flutter IDE while native breakpoints stop in the native IDE.

questions.q: A screen is janky. How do you find the cause?
questions.a: Run a profile build on a real device and open DevTools Performance. Slow frames show whether the UI thread (build and layout in Dart) or the raster thread (painting) is over budget. For UI I track widget rebuilds and profile the CPU; for raster I look for large images, clipping, opacity layers and shader compilation.

questions.q: How do you debug a RenderFlex overflow?
questions.a: Select the widget in the Inspector and read the layout explorer: it shows the constraints the Row or Column received and the sizes its children asked for. The fix is usually Expanded or Flexible on the child that should shrink, or making the content scrollable.

questions.q: Why measure performance in profile mode and not debug?
questions.a: Debug mode runs with assertions and a JIT compiler and is several times slower than what users get. Profile mode is compiled like release but keeps the hooks DevTools needs, so its numbers are realistic.

questions.q: What is launch.json?
questions.a: The file in .vscode that tells VS Code how to start or attach to a program for debugging: the debugger type, launch or attach, the program or port, arguments and environment variables. It is checked into the repo so the team shares the same setup.

questions.q: How do you work safely with an AI coding agent?
questions.a: Give it a narrow task with the files named and a way to verify. Ask for a plan before edits on anything large. Read every diff before accepting it, run the tests myself, and keep changes in small commits so a bad turn is easy to undo. I never paste secrets, and I treat its output as a draft from a colleague.

questions.q: Where do you keep project conventions for an AI assistant?
questions.a: In a rules file that the tool reads automatically, such as .cursor/rules or CLAUDE.md, checked into the repo. It holds build commands, patterns to copy and things never to touch, so they are not repeated in every prompt.

questions.q: What is the difference between user and workspace settings?
questions.a: User settings apply to every project on my machine. Workspace settings live in the repo's .vscode folder, apply to that project only, are shared with the team and override user settings.

questions.q: How do you find out what is using port 8080?
questions.a: lsof -nP -iTCP:8080 -sTCP:LISTEN prints the process and its PID. Then kill PID asks it to stop, and kill -9 PID forces it if it does not.

questions.q: What is the difference between | and > ?
questions.a: A pipe sends one command's output into another command as its input. A redirect sends output to a file: > overwrites, >> appends. 2>&1 sends error output to the same place as normal output.

questions.q: What is the difference between kill and kill -9?
questions.a: kill sends SIGTERM, which asks the process to shut down and lets it clean up. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which the process cannot catch, so it stops immediately without cleanup. I try the first before the second.

questions.q: What does PATH do?
questions.a: It is the list of folders the shell searches, in order, to find a program when I type its name. 'command not found' usually means the tool's folder is missing from PATH, and which name shows which copy would run.

questions.q: An API call fails in the browser. Where do you look?
questions.a: The Network panel. I check the status code, the request URL and headers, the request payload and the response body. A CORS error shows in the Console with the header that is missing. Copy as cURL lets me replay it outside the browser to separate a client problem from a server one.

questions.q: What is the difference between 401 and 403?
questions.a: 401 means the server does not know who I am: the credentials are missing, expired or invalid. 403 means it knows who I am and I am not allowed to do this.

questions.q: What are Postman environments for?
questions.a: They hold the values that differ between servers, such as base URL and test account, so one saved request works against local, QA and production by switching a dropdown. Secrets belong in the vault or as sensitive values, not in a shared collection.

questions.q: How do you test that an API still works after a change?
questions.a: Tests on each request that assert status and the fields I depend on, grouped in a collection that runs in order: log in, save the token, create, read, clean up. The same collection runs from the command line in CI on every build.

questions.q: How do you debug a Spring Boot request?
questions.a: Start the app in debug, put a thread-suspending breakpoint on the controller method, send the request and step from controller to service to repository. I evaluate repository calls while paused and turn on SQL logging to see the query that actually ran.

questions.q: How do you debug a service running in Docker or on a remote machine?
questions.a: Start the JVM with the JDWP agent listening on a port, publish or forward that port, and connect from the IDE with a Remote JVM Debug configuration. The IDE needs the same source version as the running build.

questions.q: A query is slow. How do you investigate?
questions.a: Run EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a safe copy) and read the plan. I look for sequential scans on large tables, a missing index on the filter or join column, and row estimates that are far from the real counts. Then I check how often the app runs it, because many fast queries in a loop is the other common cause.

questions.q: What precautions do you take when connecting a tool to a production database?
questions.a: A read-only user and a read-only connection, manual transactions so nothing commits by accident, a row limit on every exploratory query, and credentials kept in a secret store rather than a project file.
